extracted.intended_audience: general public / news readers interested in culture, entertainment, and current events
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards about making or publishing humor (especially on social media) about tragedies or sensitive events, aimed at public figures, corporate spokespeople, and publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid joking about crises or tragedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Joking about the crisis in Japan isn't turning out to be so funny for some.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article treats humor about disasters as socially unacceptable in this context and gives examples (Gilbert Gottfried, 50 Cent) where such jokes provoked backlash. Implicit guidance: do not make jokes about recent disasters or events that have caused loss of life or widespread suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial standard — do not republish offensive lines
rubrics_metrics.description: We're not going to repost any of what Gottfried said because the lines don't meet this blog's standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers may refuse to reproduce offensive material even when reporting on it; when content 'doesn't meet [the blog's] standards,' omit the actual offensive wording while reporting the incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider corporate ties and business impacts before making or repeating jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Aflac, by the way, does about 75 percent of its business in Japan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public figures or brand partners should factor a company's business relationships and market exposure into whether certain jokes are appropriate; insensitive remarks that offend a key market can lead to termination of endorsement/voice roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/off-color jokes can lead to job loss or resignation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedian Gilbert Gottfried has lost his job as the voice of the Aflac duck ... Mississippi Gov. Haley Barbour has accepted his press spokesman's resignation after the aide sent around two 'off-color' jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both public-facing jokes (tweets) and internally circulated off-color jokes can have professional consequences. Implicit rule: avoid off-color humor in official, semi-official, or workplace communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shock-value defense does not insulate from criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of my tweets are ignorant I do it for shock value. Hate it or love it. I'm cool either way.' — 50 Cent
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming 'shock value' or ignorance as a rationale for offensive humor is a common defense but may not prevent backlash; entertainers may later issue sympathy or clarification statements, but the initial harm/reaction can persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public apology is the expected remediation but may not reverse consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Today, Gottfried went back on Twitter to apologize. 'I meant no disrespect, and my thoughts are with the victims and their families,' he says.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuing an apology and expressing sympathy for victims is the standard immediate response after offensive remarks. The article shows apologies occur but does not imply they always restore relationships or employment.
